entries.meaning: As Hanuman was leaving, Sita gave him her crest-jewel; Rama takes that very jewel and presses it to his heart. With both eyes full of tears, Hanuman conveys Janaka's daughter's words: she clasps the Lord's feet together with Lakshmana's and asks why he has abandoned one devoted to those feet in mind, deed, and speech. She admits one fault: though separated from him, her life did not depart. Her eyes are to blame, for their tears preserve the body from separation's fire. Her vast distress needs no telling to the compassionate Lord. Each instant passes like an age; he should come quickly, conquer the wicked host by the strength of his arms, and bring her home.

Hearing of Sita's sorrow, Rama, the abode of joy, fills his lotus eyes with tears. He asks how adversity could touch even in a dream anyone whose sole recourse in speech, body, and mind is him. Hanuman replies that adversity exists only when remembrance and worship of the Lord cease. The demons are a small matter: they will defeat the foe and bring Janaki. Rama says no god, human, sage, or embodied being has benefited him as Hanuman has; his mind cannot face the debt with any matching return. He can see no way to become debt-free. Gazing again and again at Hanuman with tearful eyes and thrilled limbs, Rama moves him deeply; Hanuman falls at his feet, overwhelmed by love, crying, 'Protect me, Lord!'

Again and again Rama tries to raise Hanuman, but absorbed in love he does not wish to rise. The Lord's lotus hand rests upon the monkey's head; recalling this state, Shiva too becomes absorbed. Regaining attention, Shiva resumes the beautiful story. Rama raises Hanuman, embraces him, takes his hand, and seats him very near. Asked how he burned Ravana-guarded, formidable Lanka, Hanuman knows the Lord is pleased and answers without pride: a monkey's great prowess is merely going from branch to branch. Leaping the sea, burning the golden city, overcoming the demon hosts, and laying waste the grove were all Rama's power, none of his own. Nothing is unattainable for one favored by the Lord; through his power even cotton can burn the submarine fire.

words.sourceRef: Sundarakanda 33, line 8; pinned witness retains बिधि

entries.note: Line 8 retains the source token बिधि; the immediate syntax suggests 'in this manner,' while the common बधि reading would mean 'having slain.'

entries.meaning: Hanuman asks the Lord for imperishable devotion, the giver of highest joy, and Rama grants it. Shiva tells Uma that one who knows Rama's nature desires no feeling apart from worship, and whoever takes this exchange to heart obtains devotion to Raghupati's feet. The monkeys hail their compassionate source of happiness. Rama summons Sugriva, asks him to prepare the march, and orders that the monkeys be mobilized without delay. The gods delight in the sight, shower flowers, and return to heaven, while Sugriva rapidly calls up troop leaders and hosts of bears and monkeys of many colors and immeasurable strength.

The mighty bears and monkeys bow at the Lord's lotus feet and roar. Rama surveys the whole army with a merciful lotus-eyed glance; empowered by his grace, the monkey chiefs seem like winged mountains. As Rama joyfully sets out, many lovely auspicious signs appear. Sita knows of his departure when her left side throbs, while the same signs become ill omens for Ravana. The limitless army advances, armed with claws and carrying mountains and trees, ranging over earth and sky. Its lion-roars make the elephants of the quarters trumpet and reel, the earth and mountains sway, and the ocean heave, while gods, sages, nagas, gandharvas, and kinnaras rejoice. The vast weight repeatedly overwhelms Shesha; gripping the tortoise's hard shell with his teeth, he seems to inscribe upon it the enduring record of Rama's beautiful march. The Lord reaches the seashore, where the warriors spread out and begin eating abundant fruit.

Ever since Hanuman burned Lanka, its demons have lived in fear and privately concluded that their lineage cannot survive: what good can come to the city when even the approaching enemy's messenger has indescribable strength? Hearing the citizens through her agents, Mandodari becomes deeply agitated. In private she clasps her husband's feet and gives advice steeped in prudence: abandon conflict with Hari, take her beneficial words to heart, and have Sita returned by a minister if he wants his own welfare. The mere recollection of Rama's messenger makes demon women miscarry. Sita has come like a cold night fatal to the lotus-grove of the demon race; unless she is returned, neither Shiva nor Brahma can secure Ravana's welfare. Rama's arrows are a mass of snakes and the demons frogs, so he should abandon obstinacy and act before they are swallowed.

The world-famous egotist hears his wife's words but laughs, declaring fear to be woman's true nature: even in an auspicious moment her unsteady mind is afraid. If the monkey army comes, he says, the poor demons will live by eating it; it is laughable that the wife of one before whom the guardians of the worlds tremble should be frightened. He laughs, embraces her, and goes to court in swollen attachment, while Mandodari worries that fate has turned against her husband. Told that the entire army has crossed the sea, Ravana asks his ministers for proper counsel. They merely laugh and suppress their judgment, boasting that he conquered gods and demons without effort and that humans and monkeys count for nothing. A minister, physician, or teacher who speaks pleasingly from fear or hope quickly destroys, respectively, kingdom, body, or dharma.

words.grammar: idiomatic element in मष्ट करि रहहू

entries.note: The pinned witness's मष्ट in the council scene is retained and marked for review; the syntax depicts ministers suppressing candid advice rather than offering an independent judgment.

entries.meaning: Such flatterers prove to be Ravana's helpers, repeatedly praising him to his face. At the right moment Vibhishana enters, bows at his brother's feet, takes his seat with permission, and offers advice suited to his understanding. Whoever desires welfare, good fame, sound judgment, an auspicious destiny, and many joys should shun another's wife as one shuns the fourth day's moon. Even a sole lord of all fourteen worlds cannot endure while acting with hostility toward living beings; no one calls even a cultivated ocean of virtues good when he has a little greed. Desire, anger, pride, and greed are paths to hell. Vibhishana urges Ravana to abandon them all and worship Raghubira, whom the saints worship.

Vibhishana explains that Rama is not a human king but the Lord of the worlds and the death even of Time: Brahman, free of affliction, unborn, all-pervading, unconquered, beginningless, and infinite. The ocean of compassion has assumed a human body for the welfare of cows, Brahmins, and gods, to delight his servants, break the wicked host, and protect Vedic dharma. Ravana should renounce enmity, bow his head, return Vaidehi to the Lord, and worship Rama, the causeless friend. Rama does not abandon one who seeks refuge even if the sins of betraying the whole world cling to that person; his name destroys the three afflictions. Vibhishana repeatedly clasps Ravana's feet and begs him to leave pride, delusion, and arrogance and worship the Lord of Kosala. He adds that sage Pulastya sent this warning through a disciple and that he has conveyed it at the first opportunity.

The wise minister Malyavan is delighted by Vibhishana's words and tells Ravana that his younger brother's policy is an ornament to him and should be held in his heart. Ravana angrily calls them both fools for proclaiming the enemy's greatness and demands that they be removed. Malyavan returns home; Vibhishana again joins his hands and says that right and perverse understanding reside in every heart, as the Puranas and Vedas declare. Where there is sound judgment there are many forms of prosperity; where there is bad judgment lies the root of calamity. Perverse thought now inhabits Ravana's heart, so that he regards benefit as harm and an enemy as beloved. His intense attachment to Sita is a death-night for the lotus-bed of the demon lineage. Clasping his feet, Vibhishana asks Ravana to preserve his affection for his younger brother: return Sita to Rama, and no harm will come to him.
